newsitem.title: INDIA: India RBI needs to create dollar demand - dealer.
newsitem.headline: India RBI needs to create dollar demand - dealer.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) needs to create dollar demand to counter the rupee's overvaluation, Moses Harding, chief dealer at Indusind Bank Ltd., said on Friday.
Speaking to Reuters Financial Television from the annual Indian Forex Club meeting in the resort state of Goa, Harding said the rupee's strength was the central bank's main concern.
"There is no question of a depreciation of the rupee unless some active measures are taken to create demand for the foreign currencies here," Harding said.

The RBI on Monday announced that foreign institutional investors will be allowed to hedge investments in Indian government debt, but Harding said he did not believe this would have a great impact on foreign currency demand.

"So probably the first measure (to create demand for foreign currency) is to allow NRIS (non-resident Indians) who have already invested in rupee deposits at a yield of 16 to 21.5 percent, so it makes sense for them to hedge their rupee assets," he said.

"And secondly for the past two years we have seen a lot of foreign currency loans, ECBS (external commercial borrowings) offtake in local market, so rupee credit offtake is absolutely zero," he added.

"So probably if the government puts a ban on availing of foreign currency advances or puts a clause that 25 to 50 percent of foreign currency loans should be hedged, then it should create a demand for the dollar," the chief dealer said.
Harding said that the current market benchmark for the dollar-rupee was 35.70 rupees. The rupee closed at 35.7125/75 on Thursday.

"So 35.70 is the benchmark and the RBI is going to continue this passive intervention (dollar buying) otherwise the rupee is going to strengthen, and definitely exporters are lobbying against the rupee getting overstrengthened," he said.
However, the RBI should abandon this intervention and allow some volatility measures in the market in order to develop a rupee derivatives market, he said.

"If you are going to look at developing a rupee-based derivative product this passive intervention should not be there because there are no volatility measures in the market, and volatility measures is one of the important phenomena (needed) to base a rupee derivatives market," he said.
Harding also noted that the central bank was paying for the huge inflows of foreign investment into India.

"That is costing more than five percent. Just to elaborate the inflows (of dollars) are parked in the Federal Reserve, by means of passive intervention, where you get a yield of six percent and it results in increasing the money supply in the local market.
"And in the sterilization process (sales of government debt to suck excess rupees out of circulation) is costing us 11 percent -- so that it is worth paying five percent for the huge inflows.
"As long as the capital inflows are going to be more than the trade deficit the rupee is going to remain strong," he said.
